I am the House of Julii.

I am to the North of Italy. I am part of the Glorious Roman Republic, sharing with three other factions; the blue Scorpios (I think) who have decided to take a couple of islands and then the big parts of Africa. The green Brutii, who decided that looking ridiculous would best show the Greeks what's what. And I, wearing fantastically imperial red, who was tasked with sorting out the dirty Gauls.

I quickly began a conquest that would put the Black Templars to shame, sending out army after army, conquering town after town. They tried to resist, but my men were worth two of theirs, and my men outnumbered their three to one. As we came, we took most of them slaves, built up my core towns, built as many temples to convince more people to shag as possible, and continued on our merry murdering way.

Occasionally, the Guals or Brittony or Germans would manage to scrape together an entire army of 2000 people. These were the battles I, and my family, were born for. We smashed together, blood and sword and sinew, as my Velites threw their spears overhead, and cavalry quickly hit them from behind. Few enemies died facing us in the north, many ran and most died with sword wounds in their backs rather than face us.

We tried peace once, and we paid the price with roman lives. When they begged for our mercy, they found only our gladius. We heard the lamentations of their women as they were taken back to mighty Arretium, our capital city. And how it had grown; on the back of slaves and the glory of our men, we raised great arenas and temples to show our glory! We raised great barracks to train our men! We grew the greatest of men to enforce our will! And the north of Europe was stained red with blood; the map of Europe was stained red with our flags.

We found that land ran out quickly; Europa gave way before our bloodlust did, and we turned to look back. We were disgusted with what we saw. Corruption. Weakness. Our supposed equals made peace with the savages, our supposed superiors hide behind the walls of Rome. They whispered of treachery, but we knew weakness and corruption when we saw it. The spineless Scorpios had no trouble gaining the favour of the Senate; spending more time on their knees in glorious Rome than sword in hand over Carthage. The Brutii failed to live up to their brutish name; content with a paltry pile of sand, growing fat and lazy as we had grown lean and numerous in both flesh and glory.

We recalled our armies to home, to the swell of the crowds. They chanted our name, and spat at the mentions of the Senate. All had been united under our banner; did not the Celts and Gauls and Germans and Thrycians alike not bend the knee to the glorious Romans, all beneath the bloody red banner of the Julii? Mars had made his favour clear; he doesn't favour cowards, and Jupiter didn't let the weak rule. We built temples in His Name, and spread his name further than even the diplomats know. All that was left was to follow the glory given to us, under the gaze of the gods and cheers of the people, we marched the final path.

All roads lead to Rome.

Classic game, it uses a realistic battle engine which simulates battles down to minute details, in a way no longer found in newer engines which depend apon flashy graphics to generate interest. The sheer effort put into this game really tells you its creators cared about it they were not just throwing something flashy out there to get as much money as possible. The game makes up for its old and ancient graphics with interesting game mechanics that you just DONT get in the newer RTS games with intricate tactical aspects in addition to intriacate strategic ones. since so much attention has been given to FPS games in recent years. The game is well made and it shows. In modern total wars and other RTS games, troops getting into 1v1 cinimatic fights where thy slide around on the map rather than recreating actual formation dynamics and combat in a believeable way as Rome 1 does. In Rome 1 TW you don't just have static groups of people fighting in one spot like other games, your troop formations collide and dudes go flying, people get knocked down. The larger force slowly pushes the smaller one back while its formation fluxuates, troops arrange sheilds to defend against attackers leaving weakspots open to well positioned archers. Every part of the strategic map is mapped out into battle maps that mirror that place on the stratiegic map. I am not talking you get a different set of cookie cutter template battle maps depending on your region NO!!! I mean the battle map is an EXACT copy of the terrain on the stategic map. You see a hill on the over all map and move your army to it so the enemy will attack you on ground you choose that hill is on the battle map valleys mountain you name it the battle is in that spot not a faximally of that spot THAT SPOT. The same goes for citys, each is unique and grows in unique ways and this shows on the siege map. Build something in a city and its on the battle map, if a saboteur destroys something it is destroyed on the battle map, Your family members/ generals grow as a result of the situations you put them in becoming complex individuals, put them in a big city with librarys and academys and they may become a soft person but a good organizer, or maybe if the city is a religious center he may become pious or slowly go insane, or become blood thirsty if you constantly send him into battle and he gets kills in said battles (yes even what he does in the battles matters). Another really cool mechanic is that when you recruit units the men are taken from the local populus and when disbanded the men generally resettle in that region! and city level is determined by population so recruit to many from a populas and the city will grow slowly while inversely you can move your populus around to level up citys. Another difference from newer games is the factions, they are few in number compared to the scores of factions in newer games but each faction in very unique, with some factions sharing cultures and others with similar but different cultures. Each culture has a unique city style ect.

RTW has an epic feel.

As of today, this game is nearly eleven years old.  So, the battle graphics are not as crisp as newer titles, the historicity of some units is sketchy (or just made up), and it seems that multiplayer is not smooth in Steam.  Fortunately, none of these mean a thing to me.  The heart of the game is in the grand strategy and the personal narrative.

With over a hundred regions in which to play, the strategic game is where RTW shines. You need to plan where you will expand and where you will defend... and then be ready to adapt when the AI does not do what you expect. You may be the pawn of the Senate and serve at their beck and call.  You might try to expand against the weak.  You can follow the trade routes to gain riches through conquest.  You will find yourself occupying regions merely to stymie your enemies (and your allies). Or you might work your way towards all seven Wonders to reap their benefits.

The twenty factions all fall into one of the major religio/cultural groupings. Some conquered peoples will not like your religion, but a few might. Some conquered peoples will happily accept you as overlord because you share the same cultural values... and the Spanish clans just don't like anyone. Some factions have great infantry, some have cavalry, and some do many things well.  Yet, you can usually find mercenaries (disgruntled locals, rival tribes, or thugs) who might fill the holes in your army.

Yes, most negative reviews harp on about the lag in multiplayer and the poor graphics in battles.  If you need gratuitous violence or managing pixels in a free for all, then watch Mad Max: Fury Road or play League of Legends. If you want to make decisions that will impact your dominion fifty turns down the road, then this game can give it to you.  What kind of temples will you build in each region... or should you let the people keep their native religion?  Will a town become a recruiting station or a cash cow?  When you conquer a region, you'll have to decide to either just incorporate it into your lands as is, relocating half the people by enslaving them, or just slaughtering most of the inhabitants and stealing their goods.... and you'll find yourself using each throughout the campaign, because one size does not fit all.

And guess what?  I don't fight the battles.  If I did, I'd never finish a campaign.  I hit the auto calculation button every time.  Why?  Well... there are a number of positions which you will fulfill in a game.  Benevolent multi-generational spirit guiding your family, governor of a province, Commander in Chief, general of an army, and captain of a unit. Playing all of these breaks the narrative for me... I play the macro game, i.e. the big picture.  I plot and scheme, I build cities, and recruit armies.  Then I send them out into the field.  How they do is up to them.  If they win... great! I must be a genius.  If they lose... nuts. Back to the drawing board.

Two friends of mine, let's call them Doc and Bro, played RTW like this... Doc played the campaign map, i.e. he decided what units were built and where the battles were fought, but Bro fought all the battles.  Doc was the CinC and Bro was the General.  They played two campaigns in three years, but they remember both as epic stories of their teamwork.

In addition to the war... campaign strategy, building armies, transportation of armies, theatres of conflict, fog of war, etc... you'll have to deal with natural disasters, (In one game, a young woman of my family married a promising young fellow, but he died a year later in an earthquake.), piracy, rebellions, brigands, bribery attempts upon your armies, old age, death in battle, adoptions, plagues (stupid unwashed barbarians), and assassination. (In one game, the youngest son of my German leader was sent to subdue Gaul and Hispania. This gave him a command of 10.  I marched him and his elite German veterans across the Alps to conquer Rome... but the Romans assassinated him.  With my hordes leaderless, the Romans proceeded to sieze Gaul and invade Germania.) All of these additional factors help create a unique narrative for each game.

Oh, and when you play as a Roman faction, you'll need to keep an eye upon the Senate... how they view you, how the plebs (the masses) view you, Senatorial missions, and the official Senatorial stance with every other faction. For instance, you may have a great trade agreement with the Egyptians and a low standing with the Senate, but the Sentate demands that you attack Egypt... attacking Egypt will hurt your income considerably, but offending the Senate may cause them to label you as a rebel... what will you do?

Certain events always happen... Aetna erupts and the plague breaks out in Macedonia, but certain other events happen only when certain triggers occur (the Marian reforms), while others, such as floods, are random.  But the big event for Roman players is the Civil War.  At some point the plebs will want you to deal with the Senate and/or at some point the Senate will either have enough of you or become paranoid of your growing power that they'll demand the head of your family to commit suicide.  If you agree, they'll do it every turn until your family ceases to exist.  If you're not ready for war, then you can comply with the Senate for a few years (and prune your family tree of bad apples in the process), but at some point you'll have to stand up to the Senate... at which point you go to war with all other Romans.  Talk about raising your anxiety.... sheesh!

All of your characters really flesh out the narrative... the story of your family.  Spies, diplomats, assassins, admirals, generals, and governors all have character traits that make them who they are.  Some will be drunkards, perverts, and ne'er do wells, while some will be loyal, moral, and cunning.  They'll also tend to generate a following of hangers on, freeloaders, men of honor, mistresses, etc...  For instance, a son might come of age in your family with a command of 3... a natural born general... but on his way to the frontier to defeat the Dacians, his inner circle grows to include a Drunken Uncle and an Actor and they decrease his command ability by 3... Ouch!  He's now a zero...

In the first two Total War games, Shogun and Medieval, you had family members, but not nearly as many as Rome.  So to help you manage them (and for the sheer fun of telling a story), RTW includes a family tree.

The game's not perfect.  The legendary/semi-mythological units can be frustrating and the Egyptians were certainly not using chariots in the second century BC. Naval combat results can make you scratch your head.  Negative income numbers on the campaign map are definitely misleading. There is always the point at which you know you've won even though you may only be forty to seventy percent of the way to the finish... but that's true of a lot of games.

There may be other games out there that have made improvements to the grand strategy game, but I've always found this one to be fun to return to.

Rome's got good combat, decent unit roosters for different cultures, good siege mechanics & decent city "building/development". You can also build forts & watch towers on the strategic map.

Rome was made before the switch to the new engine, which means that each individual unit actually fight on an individual level, trying to hit enemies & block incoming attacks, instead of the crazy 1v1 kill-animation system. This have a major effect on how battles turn out & how they're conducted. If you got more units of similar skill & situation, they tend to do a fair bit better, instead of it just being a battle of attrition. Projectiles are fairly strong, but as far as I can tell, don't home-in on targets & ready, large shields greatly negate their effectiveness.

I should mention that the music is the best in this title by a land-slide, it's always fitting & it's always get's you in the right mood for the situation.

The one thing you may miss in this if you're used to the later titles is the naval combat, it's automated in Rome. Also, the graphics are very dated. Camera controls are janky & visual feedback is poor compared to later titles.

Compared to the other Total War titles, there's only 3 other games that even come close to being as good as this one: Shogun 2, Medieval 2 & Empire(after milions of patches). I haven't played enough Warhammer to tell how it hold's up yet, but it looks promising.

OBS!
You may get random crashes to desktop if you buy it through steam, unless you go to the main folder, select everything, put it in a new folder within the main folder & then check integrity of the game & let it re-download everything. The game should then not crash, probably, it worked for me (I use Windows 7).

WARNING FOR WINDOWS 10 USERS AND POSSIBLE OTHERS: The game got a post-Gamespy update that will cause the game to do all kinds of crazy display stuff and crash. What you need to do is turn off anti-aliasing by default by going into the game's installation folder, preferences folder, then preferences file and make sure AA_QUALITY says AA_QUALITY:AA_ OFF. This should let you launch the game. If you wish to turn on AA from there, you can do so in NVIDIA Control Panel or any other equivalent program, as turning it back on in the menus will cause it to crash again.

IF YOU GET REALLY BAD FRAMERATES AND LAGGY INPUT NO MATTER YOUR SPECS: Right-click the game in your library, click properties, then click Set Launch Options. In the text box, type the three characters "-ne" without the quotes and press okay. This should fix that problem for most people out there.

With that done, I'd like to say that although this game is a bit primitive compared to modern TW games, it still can be a very fun game.  

Pros:

-The Campaign map is very no frills compared to modern TW games. You can build any building in any city, public disorder is easy to maintain, and it just lacks feature bloat of later games. The game is all about the battles, something I'd wish would come back after games like Attila.

- The battles can look and play better than modern TW games in some ways. Losing units will actually be beaten back and enveloped by superior forces, soldiers will respond to orders at different times, and the engagements can have some real clash and weight to them. 

-There's actually strategy to the strategy map. I wasn't a huge fan of M2/Empire/Napoleon/Attila's maps because they tended to have lots of wide open plains, while Rome 1+2 and Shogun 2 had lots of limiting terrain features where you could create chokepoints and use terrain like mountains and rivers to your advantage.

Cons:

-Battles can be over a little too quickly. I kind of get whiplash at how fast I go from marching, to melee, to routing an enemy army.

-The flipside to things like independent unit movement is that response can be sluggish, sometimes often so bad that I can't tell if the game knows if I ordered them to do anything.

-Pathfinding can be garbage sometimes, especially in cities.

-You can still get cascade moments where your empire is powerful enough that you're just auto-resolving your way across large swaths of the map at some points.

Overall, I was surprised by how much I enjoyed the game despite not playing it since roughly around its launch. Once you get over some usability issues, there's a game here that's aged better than it has any right to.

Rome Total War Checklist:

1. Has good AI? Check.
2. Has good mod support? Check.
3. Has no DLC? Check.
4. Has an actual challenge? Check.
5. Has an Expansion worth playing? Check. 
6. Has the feeling of reward from success? Check.

Conclusion: They don't make games like this anymore. Stay away from Sega and CA's newer cash cows.

Often considered to be one of the best games in the Total War series. Rome is a game that has captured my heart and imagination since i first saw my friends played the game on his computer back in 2006. There is so much in the grand ambition of this game that far exceed most games back in 2004.

At the start of the game, you start out with the Roman faction. You have 3 major families to choose from; The Julii to the north, The Scipii to the south, and The Brutii to the southeast. rosterwise, there are no difference between all 3 families. Instead, each family is given different objectives by the senate to capture land for the roman republic. Your ultimate goal would be to gather enough strength and the support of the people to eventually overthrow the senate and become Emperor of Rome. After you complete the game, you will then be given the opportunity to play several other factions who are also vying for power in ancient Europe which spices up the gameplay with their different units and tactics.

Gameplaywise, the game is divided into 2 phases. The map phase has you in a turn based gameplay where you manage your empire to gain funds, act in diplomacy, look after your cities, and build up your army to expand and defend your territory. When a battle starts, the battle phase begins which follows an RTS formula. These are the true highlights of the game as you control armies up to thousands of troops on screen to defeat your opponents,

On the positives, this game aims to be grand scale in its endevours which for the most part succeeds. The feeling you get as you march your army of legionnares to conquer the Gauls or sacking Carthage is unmatch by any other game outside of the Total War series. Battles are often won with wit rather than force. Due to how the game's battle system that attempts to be more realistic with troop morale and the like, often times you can win or lose battles depending more on how you strategize and predict what your opponent will do next. Nothing is quite as exciting as being overwhelmed by number of your enemy soldiers only to outsmart them with a well place flank attack and gaining a heroic victory as a result. Rome succeeds at both giving the player the feeling of being a general and a conqueror that other strategy games don't really give. This is only exemplified by the excellent soundtrack composed by Jeff van Dyck which gives out a an ancient and haunting feel throughout the experience.

On to the negatives, one of the biggest issue that is incredibly infamous in the Total War series in general is the AI. Generally the AI can be competent but often times are rather stupid. Most fights can be easily won by just doing a flank attack and the AI will have no clue what to do. If you're looking for competent foes to fight then you're better off playing the multiplayer instead. The game has a glaring issue with its diplomacy system. The game is often unclear with what the other faction wants and they often come off as acting erratic rather than clever. Your allies may suddenly declare war on you for no reason and you're stuck with sudden attacks despite just a moment ago they proposed an alliance with you. Another weird hiccup is how the roster is designed. It's pretty clear that the Roman faction was given the most attention considering the name of the game, but other factions feel underdeveloped, severely in some more than others as a result. The game's factions are clearly unbalanced as a result and playing as them in the campaign can feel very frustrating especially if you play as one of the factions who are at war against Rome. Because the Roman faction is basically 4 factions with their own funds and AI, playing against them often feels more annoying than fun as you are severely overwhelmed by them if you don't act first. One minor issue i have is more towards historical accuracy. While the romans were given attention to reflect their historical design, the other factions caters more towards stereotypes that makes the whole thing feel cartoony instead. (The worst example of this is the Egyptians who despite at the time was more Greek than Egyptian as part of the legacy of Alexander the Great, CA opted to make them the stereotype egyptian from pre-Alexander time which makes no sense whatsoever).

Overall, Rome Total War is a game that is just incredible in what it accomplishes, while the game has plenty of blemishes that are more visible now than ever, it's not enough to diminish how much of an impact this game created. Follow that with the game had a very vibrant modding community in its hayday that iron out those issues and you have a game that i recommend for just about any strategy fan who are into ancient warfare with thousands of soldiers on screen battling each other.

Rome: Total War. One of my all-time favorite games. Taking place in the late Roman Republic, you assume control of one of three Roman families vying for power. Depending on which family you select, the Senate will usually direct you against one of three adversaries - the Greeks, the Gauls, or the Carthaginians. The beautiful thing about Total War, however, is you can simply ignore the Senators and go on a campaign of your own... Egyptians? Invade them! Is the Senate demanding you join in on the war against the Macedon, but you'd rather become allies? Go for it! Just make sure you keep a home guard, because Civil War is a constant threat!

It has been almost ten years since Rome's release. It hasn't aged terribly bad - the AI is somewhat atrocious, the graphics are dated, but the game is still genuinely satisfying. At the price Rome goes for during Steam's seasonal sales, there's really no excuse NOT to give this game a try. If nothing else, it is a taste of nostalgia before these types of games became more like movies and less like free-for-all sandboxes!

Well.....reviewing this game is hard. For it's time, it was without a doubt one of, if not the greatest, strategy games of all time. However, comparing it to newer Total Wars (except for ROME II, that is something else entirely) it lacks in several things, notably historical accuracy, diplomacy, and managing your government. 

For one, in historical accuracy, there are multiple nations (like Gaul, Spain, Greece, etc.) that are unified nations even though in real life they were a divided people, with seperate clans, city states, etc., but for some reason CA mashed a lot of city states and tribes together to form unified nations, which is completely inaccurate. Also, in Egypt is not Hellenistic at ALL. They still have traditional Egyptian paganism as their religion, and their units are traditional Egyptian ones, even though Egypt was now practically a Middle Eastern copy of Greece thanks to Alexander the Great. 

In diplomacy, there are very few options (some examples are trade rights, alliance, and map info), which lessens your interactions with other nations. The AI also struggles to properly conduct diplomacy.

Finally, there is governemnt. For Roman factions, the Republic government is somewhat accurately displayed, but in general, there really is no "government system" like in some later Total Wars, although there is a family tree that allows you to set the faction heir, adding a bit of spice to government. 

If we put those those things aside, though, you will find a true classic of a strategy game-and I'm pretty sure most people here would agree with me. In a time where graphics made people look like horrible mutants, the AI was as smart as your neighborhood stray dog, and strategy games lacked a lot of actual strategy, this game was revolutionary. The graphics, although inferior to today's games, probably looked really great to a lot of players back in 2004.  The jump from the previous Total War, Medieval, to Rome in terms of graphics was absoultely stunning. The AI (which, to be honest, is not much smarter than the neighborhood stray) is competent despite occasional errors. Diplomacy, while lacking in true immersion, adds a new level of strategy to the game despite its simplicity. The government system, while being very basic, also adds to the strategy of the game, as you scramble to find a sutiable heir for your glorious (or, more often than not, not-so-glorious) empire. 

Speaking of empires, there are 20 factions, with about half of them playable, half of them not playable. Technically, there is a 21st faction: the rebels. The rebels not only represent actual rebels, which I am perfectly okay with, but they also represent "minor factions" that CA left out of the game, which is kinda sloppy to me. However, all-in-all, the campaign is sound, if perhaps a tad disappointing to modern gamers. 

Now, on to battles. It is usually not possible to manage a nation without going to war occasionally, and this game certainly does not oppose that statement. You will end up in countless battles, usually with random weaklings who think they are better than you, but you will sometimes find yourself matched against a worthy foe. If it is a land battle, you can do one of three things: fight the battle out on a battle map, have the computer auto-resolve the battle, or retreat. For naval battles, you only really have the auto resolve option. For the battle map, you and everyone involved, regardless of whether they are on your side or not, will command various units that can be trained in cities if you have the proper buildings (in the campaign). You lead these soldiers to victory or defeat against the enemy. I personally believe CA did a great job with the battle mechanic of the game.

If you like Total War games, strategy games in general, video games in general, or if you like life, then buy this game. Even if you don't like life, still buy it. This is a true classic of a strategy game, and you would be a fool to pass on it if you are a fan of the genre.

Overall, 9/10.

Also, this game definitely deserves the "Test of Time" award. An absolute classic of the strategy genre.

This game honestly did not really need a remaster. It plays perfectly fine. I do like that the remaster made every faction playable, but to honest not every faction in this game is worth playing. The problems are with many of the cultures unit roster being reduced to generic often ahistorical rosters making some of them not fun at all to play. Say what you want about how bad Rome 2's implementation of the Illyrians were, they at least got a distinct roster and were unique to play.

I generally consider Rome 2 a much better game, but there are a few things this game does better. The settlement building trees in this game are simplified compared to Rome 2, but also make much more sense. Rome 2 had annoying settlement building mechanics where different mutually exclusive buildings gave incredibly minor differences in benefits and it made it sometimes feel like you had to sit around with a calculator to determine if it's even worth it to build up certain settlements, let alone in which way. Rome 1 only had that issue with temple buildings, which I find perfectly fine. 

Rome 1 also generally plays "faster", which is both a positive and a negative depending on your preference. I feel like it's a lot easier to complete several turns and actually get into the battles in Rome 1, although part of that is due to Rome 1 having fewer mechanics overall. However even the battles are much faster. Oftentimes a single cavalry charge can initiate a mass rout vs an otherwise equal force of enemies, especially vs "barbarians". Units mostly lack "hit points" as well, so once an attack is determined to "hit", they die, which overall makes combat faster. They also don't "lock" into fight animations like in Rome 2, which tends to look less impressive, but also plays out much faster as several units can gang up on otherwise engaged enemy units. 

Rome 1 is also much less buggy than Medieval 2, and it just generally feels more polished than other games in the series until around Napoleon or Shogun 2. 

However it's age causes some issues. Civil war mechanics don't exist in the series yet, so they simulate it by splitting Rome into 4 factions, which leads to "Green" Roman armies running around, looking ridiculous. There also aren't a whole lot of factions, and the rosters for the ones they do have are pathetic. Overall there aren't a whole lot of mechanics either. The remaster adds merchants to the game, but agents wouldn't really hit their stride until Shogun 2. There's also no ability trees, researches, or anything like that. What there is however is a trait system for generals, causing them to have various benefits or negatives from personal things in their lives such as being an alcoholic. This is kind of close to a similar "trait" mechanic from the Warhammer games, but generals in this game could easily have like 10-15 traits depending on what they have been doing, making each one feel pretty unique.

Overall a good game. The remaster is "better", but it's a huge resource hog and is costly. Sad that this version is no longer on Steam.

What could by some measures be called the greatest game ever released in the Total War series, it has graphics that some would consider out-dated, but its bellicose yet optimistic atmosphere evocative of a small kingdom or republic fighting and building its way to greatness and founding the world's most illustrious empire is combined with game mechanics and a user interface that are easy to understand and enjoy, allowing immersion in an experience that, by the testimony of many, will be relished and entirely unforgettable to players and observers of all ages.  As opposed to the all-too-common modern model of an addiction creator with expensive DLC required just to unlock its intended features, this is a product with nigh-unrivaled replayability, fully complete from the very beginning.  
I am very unhappy that this great classic game can now only be obtained by purchasing the recent remaster, which fails to come up to its standard in most regards since it (the remaster) attempts to fix what was never broken in the first place in terms of the user interface, contributing only to compatibility and graphical quality in any significant way.  As of the date of this review, the community still strives to persuade the remaster's developers to fix or add features, but let's face it: the original is hard to beat, and every departure that is not a direct improvement seems to have rendered the remaster a second-rate copy whose greatest value is in that it is now the only way one may purchase the actual classic game or, in the case of those with compatibility issues, acquire a close approximation to it.

EDIT 01-30-2022: I am withdrawing my complaints against Total War: Rome Remastered.  A patch released within the last couple of months has allowed players to have a larger and more helpful UI reminiscent of the original game if they so desire and fixed a large number of other issues while also adding a plethora of modding tools that makes the Remaster the most moddable installation of the Total War series to date by a vast margin.  I appreciate the efforts of the developers at Feral Interactive to address the community's concerns and to further open up new possibilities for the game, some of which were not even requested but add worlds of potential and will undoubtedly make the Remaster a lasting classic, a worthy successor to the original.  
One other note:  The hours I have logged in the Steam version of Rome: Total War are the tip of the iceberg.  I played untold thousands of hours on the CD version over the years before I acquired the Steam version, all memorable and thoroughly relished, often in the company of friends and family.

Also, your generals get "perks" based on the way you use them. If, for instance, you fight the same faction multiple battles with a general, he is likely to a "perk" against that faction. Rome: Total War was epic defined and the ante was upped with Barbarian Invasion as the barbarians you had previously steamrolled were now an actually intimidating force. Creative Assembly made such a great product that it was considered by a majority in the Total War community to be the best in the series for over 10 years. And while many consider Shogun 2 to be Creative Assembly's finest achievement, it really wasn't Attila and Warhammer that Rome Total War finally lost its top spot in public opinion. Even still, this getting close to 20 year old game is still ranked in the top 5 of virtually every list of Total War games I have stumbled across.

Why? Because first and foremost the game is simple fun. Yeah it was definitely revolutionary, but it was just so fun and epic, and that is why I and so many others love and continue to love it. The horrible launch of Rome 2 and the crummy monetization of that game also gave the original new life and appreciation, and it continues to this day. People still actively play multiplayer although the community is small, and mods are still supported although they can be a bit of a hassle to download and work since there is no direct Steam support.

This game is by far, my favorite game. Hands down, no competition. It is old, but I've yet to see any other strategy game come close to this. The graphics are decent, considering its age. The gameplay is complex enough to not be bored and just steamroll through everything, yet simple enough to actually know how to use every feature this game has to offer. 

The game is basically you controlling a faction during the time of the Roman Republic, and trying to become the best nation. Diplomacy is simple and allies will betray you constantly, unless you would just completely dominate them (and even then, they still might attack you!) The AI is pretty simple to defeat, their entire strategy seems to be just throwing all of their units at you and seeing who wins. 

The challenges come when you get into the Roman Civil War. This is an in-game event where the 4 roman factions fight each other for control of Rome. Up until this point, you've just been steamrolling through barbarians with your heavy legionnaires. Once the Civil War starts, you're fighting 3 other roman factions (2 of which have just as much land as you if not more, each) and they have the same troops as you. If you're not playing a roman faction then this will never happen, but it's called ROME total war for a reason. 

If you're into strategy games, buy this game. Even if you're not, you should at least give it a try. The controls might be difficult to use at first, but the tutorial is very helpful. You will probably lose your first few campaigns, but once you get the hang of the game it will be so much fun.

I remember the first time I lost Gaul. Not the whole province — just a small town near the Rhine, some nameless village the AI called "Barbarian Camp." I stared at the map for an hour. Then I saved, loaded, and made sure it never happened again.

That was twenty years ago. I have not left since.

The first thing that hits you is the UI. God, the UI. You open the economics panel for the first time and a wall of numbers crashes over you like a Roman trireme hitting a Gallic longship. You want to know your gold income. You want to know your food. You want to know why your general is sitting in a tent doing nothing while a rebellion brews three provinces east. You have to dig through five nested menus to find out. You want to throw your tablet through a window. You do not throw it. You are a rational emperor. You build a road from Lugdunum to Massilia instead, because the grain shipments were late, and you tell yourself that is the problem. It is not the problem. The problem is that the menu that shows your trade income is a spreadsheet from 1997 wearing a toga.

You learn to live with it. You build muscle memory. You stop reading the numbers and start feeling them. A province that should be green is yellow. Something is wrong. You dig. You find a rebel general with four pikes and a grudge. You send a legion. It takes three turns. It should have taken one. The AI does not understand urgency. The AI does not understand that Rome does not negotiate with a man who has set fire to your granary. The AI makes him sit in his little barbarian camp for twenty turns, sipping his mead, while you build a second road because you are an emperor and you do not waste a road. Then, on turn twenty-one, he is at your capital. You did not see him coming. You never see them coming.

The battles are where the story actually lives, and where the game earns every hour. Eighty units on a field. The legion holds. The auxilia peel the flanks. The archers spit arrows like rain. And then — finally, after one or two stupid cavalry charges that make you grip the mouse like you want to strangle your own general — the rear breaks. You do not feel like a player. You feel like a general watching his plan work. The scale still beats most modern titles. The weight of it. The way a broken line cascades. The way morale cracks and a whole unit just turns around and runs while you are still trying to figure out where the damn river is.

And the river. Right. The elephants. I have watched elephants walk into a river in this game more times than I have watched the sunrise. Every single time. Without fail. I have a general named Marcus Aurelius who has lost three campaigns to his own elephants deciding that water is a good idea. I do not yell at the screen. I am a rational emperor. I simply note in the campaign log: "The elephants are dead. The river wins again."

The late game is where the story gets quiet. You control eighty percent of the map. The wars are over. The cultures are Roman. The roads are built. And now you are moving numbers. You are waiting for the next rebellion. You are staring at a map that is almost entirely your own color and wondering if there is anything left to do. There is. There is always something left to do. You just have to scroll through six menus to find it.

I have played modern strategy games that are prettier, smoother, and more polished. None of them give me the feeling of looking at a fully Romanized map from Britain to Mesopotamia and knowing I built this. Every road. Every culture. Every war. My hands. My mistakes. My elephants.

Vale. I have another siege to run.

This is a perfect classic of the Total War series. In short, you have the following:

1) a huge map.
2) massive armies.
3) unlimited options when it comes to planning out your campaign.

There is so much more I could mention that makes this game great, but I'd hate to write an entire novel about it. Just know that it sets a nice atmosphere and it's a great strategy game.

However, keep note of a few annoying things:

-Path finding for units can be very lousy sometimes, and there are some glitches routing as well. If a unit is defending the walls in a siege battle and they panic and route, they don't actually route for real. They just stand around idle all the time until someone kills them all off. 

-The AI, no matter how much of an effort you make, can be incredibly stupid at times. This is a trait common in all of the Total War games, but it shouldn't be too awful except for siege battles.

Otherwise, this game is definitely a classic of the TW series. The pros greatly outweigh the cons.

Unit diversity really means something in this game. as does terrain. Manually control your battles, and if you know what you're doing, you can win some major upsets. Pick the right location, set up your lines properly,  strategize. If you're lazy or overconfident, you'll end up slaughtered pretty quickly.
